*Statement figure (CL4.pdf, p. 1, cropped): cascade of aerofoils $L$ apart; the dashed control volume ($\Sigma_1$ to $\Sigma_5$) and the handwritten notes belong to the official sheet*

Source: CL4.pdf (page 1). Notes.pdf, Chapter 3: integral mass balance Eq. 3.11, integral momentum balance Eq. 3.36, integral total energy balance Eq. 3.46, force on a body Eq. 3.32.

chunks.t: Problem - CL4 Cascade of Aerofoils
chunks.x:
- Steady planar flow through an infinite array of identical aerofoils (pitch $L$), so the flow is periodic in $y$; uniform far upstream (1) and far downstream (2).
- Neglect $\bar{g}$; aerofoils thermally insulated; compressible fluid. Viscous stresses and heat conduction negligible in the uniform sections.
- Perfect gas: $h = e + \frac{p}{\rho} = c_pT = \frac{c_p}{R_g}\frac{p}{\rho} = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}\frac{p}{\rho}$ (with $p = \rho R_gT$ and $\gamma = c_p/c_v$), as in the class solution.
- Data: $[p_1,\ \rho_1,\ v_{1x},\ L,\ F_x,\ F_y]$ and, for the perfect gas of the official solution, $\gamma$ (not in the statement). Unknowns: $[p_2,\ \rho_2,\ v_{2x},\ v_{2y}]$: four equations are needed.

| Symbol | Meaning | SI unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $p_1$, $\rho_1$, $v_{1x}$ | upstream state | Pa, kg/m$^3$, m/s |
| $p_2$, $\rho_2$, $v_{2x}$, $v_{2y}$ | downstream state | Pa, kg/m$^3$, m/s |
| $L$ | pitch of the array | m |
| $F_x$, $F_y$ | force on each aerofoil per unit length | N/m |
| $\gamma$ | specific-heat ratio of the gas (perfect gas, introduced in the solution) | 1 |

chunks.t: Problem - CL4 Cascade of Aerofoils
chunks.h: Phase 2: Frames, Control Volume and Surfaces
chunks.x:
- Frame fixed to the array; $\bar{e}_x$ along the incoming stream, $\bar{e}_y$ along the array. Fixed control volume, $\bar{v}_c = 0$, one period high.
- Surfaces: $\Sigma_1$ (far upstream, height $L$, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_2$ (far downstream, height $L$, $\bar{n} = +\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_{l1}$ and $\Sigma_{l2}$ (upper and lower stream surfaces, $\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n} = 0$), $\Sigma_w$ (aerofoil surface, $\bar{v} = 0$, insulated).
- Periodicity: $\Sigma_{l2}$ is $\Sigma_{l1}$ shifted by $-L\bar{e}_y$ with opposite normals, so the integrals of any periodic quantity over $\Sigma_{l1}$ and $\Sigma_{l2}$ cancel each other out.

*Control volume of the solution (as in the class notes): $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$ (sections of height $L$), the stream surfaces $\Sigma_{l1}$ and $\Sigma_{l2}$ ($\Sigma_{l2}$ is $\Sigma_{l1}$ shifted by $-L\bar{e}_y$, so their fluxes cancel) and the aerofoil surface $\Sigma_w$. The official figure calls them $\Sigma_1$, $\Sigma_2$, $\Sigma_3$, $\Sigma_4$ and $\Sigma_5$*

Force on each aerofoil (per unit length), with $\bar{n}$ the outward normal of the control volume:

$$ \boxed{\,\bar{F} = F_x\bar{e}_x + F_y\bar{e}_y = \int_{\Sigma_w}p\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma - \int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma\,} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL4 Cascade of Aerofoils
chunks.x:
**Mass (Notes Eq. 3.11)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\,(\bar{v} - \underbrace{\cancel{\bar{v}_c}}_{0})\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma = 0 $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $\rho_1(-v_{1x})\,L$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\rho_2\,v_{2x}\,L$ |
| $\Sigma_{l1},\ \Sigma_{l2}$ | $0$ (stream surfaces) |
| $\Sigma_w$ | $0$ (wall) |

$$ \boxed{\,\rho_1v_{1x} = \rho_2v_{2x}\,} \tag{1} $$

**Linear momentum (Notes Eq. 3.36)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{v}\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \underbrace{\cancel{\bar{v}_c}}_{0})\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}p\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect } \bar{g}} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

chunks.t: Problem - CL4 Cascade of Aerofoils
chunks.x:
| Surface | $\int\rho\bar{v}\,(\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int p\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $\rho_1v_{1x}\bar{e}_x(-v_{1x})L$ | $+p_1L\,\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\rho_2(v_{2x}\bar{e}_x + v_{2y}\bar{e}_y)\,v_{2x}L$ | $-p_2L\,\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_{l1} + \Sigma_{l2}$ | $0$ | $0$ (cancel each other out) | $0$ (cancel each other out) |
| **$\Sigma_w$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_w}p\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

Boxed $\Sigma_w$ terms: $-\bar{F} = -F_x\bar{e}_x - F_y\bar{e}_y$. With (1), $\rho_2v_{2x}L = \rho_1v_{1x}L$ in the $\Sigma_2$ flux.

$$ \boxed{\,F_x = \rho_1v_{1x}L\,(v_{1x} - v_{2x}) + (p_1 - p_2)\,L\,}\ \ \text{(2)}\qquad \boxed{\,F_y = -\rho_1v_{1x}L\,v_{2y}\,}\ \ \text{(3)} $$

**Total energy (Notes Eq. 3.46)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)dV}}_{0} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\left(e + \frac{v^2}{2}\right)(\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\cdot\bar{v}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect}} - \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}(Q_c + Q_r)\,dV}}_{0} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL4 Cascade of Aerofoils
chunks.x:
Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)(\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $\rho_1\left(e_1 + \tfrac{v_{1x}^2}{2}\right)(-v_{1x})L$ | $+p_1v_{1x}L$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\rho_2\left(e_2 + \tfrac{v_{2x}^2 + v_{2y}^2}{2}\right)v_{2x}L$ | $-p_2v_{2x}L$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_{l1} + \Sigma_{l2}$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ (cancel each other out) | $0$ (cancel each other out) |
| $\Sigma_w$ | $0$ | $0$ ($\bar{v} = 0$) | $0$ ($\bar{v} = 0$) | $0$ (insulated) |

Moving the pressure work to the left turns $e$ into $h = e + p/\rho$; dividing by $\rho_1v_{1x}L = \rho_2v_{2x}L$ and using $h = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p}{\rho}$:

$$ \boxed{\,\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}\left(\frac{p_2}{\rho_2} - \frac{p_1}{\rho_1}\right) + \frac{v_{2x}^2 + v_{2y}^2}{2} - \frac{v_{1x}^2}{2} = 0\,} \tag{4} $$

(1) to (4) are four equations for the four unknowns $p_2$, $\rho_2$, $v_{2x}$, $v_{2y}$, which answers the question.

chunks.t: Problem - CL4 Cascade of Aerofoils
chunks.h: Phase 4: Interpretation, Limits and Dimensional Check
chunks.x:
- (3): the transverse force on an aerofoil equals minus the $y$ momentum given to the stream; the flow is deflected opposite to the force. (2) splits the streamwise force into a pressure drop and a momentum change.
- $\bar{F} = 0$: (1) to (4) are satisfied by state 2 = state 1. Incompressible limit ($\rho_2 = \rho_1$): $v_{2x} = v_{1x}$ and $p_1 - p_2 = F_x/L$.
- Dimensions (SI): $[F_x/L] = \text{Pa} = [\rho_1v_{1x}^2]$; $[\rho_1v_{1x}Lv_{2y}] = \text{N/m}$; $[\gamma p/((\gamma-1)\rho)] = \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2 = [v^2]$.
- Agreement with the official solution and the class solution: the same four equations (1) to (4).

chunks.t: Problem - CL4 Cascade of Aerofoils
chunks.h: Phase 4: Interpretation, Limits and Dimensional Check
chunks.x:
Extension (beyond the official solution): closed solution
With $m = \rho_1v_{1x}$: $\rho_2 = m/v_{2x}$, $v_{2y} = -F_y/(mL)$ and $p_2 = P - m\,v_{2x}$ with $P = p_1 + mv_{1x} - F_x/L$. Substituting into (4), with $E = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p_1}{\rho_1} + \frac{v_{1x}^2}{2}$ and the coefficient $\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1} = -\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}$ of $v_{2x}^2$: $(\gamma + 1)v_{2x}^2 - 2\gamma\frac{P}{m}v_{2x} + 2(\gamma - 1)\left(E - \frac{v_{2y}^2}{2}\right) = 0$. For $\bar{F} = 0$ one root is $v_{2x} = v_{1x}$; the root continuous with it is the physical one. Check: $p_1 = 101325$ Pa, $\rho_1 = 1.2$ kg/m$^3$, $v_{1x} = 100$ m/s, $L = 0.2$ m, $F_x = 30$ N/m, $F_y = -80$ N/m, $\gamma = 1.4$ give $v_{2x} = 100.16$ m/s, $v_{2y} = 3.3333$ m/s, $\rho_2 = 1.19808$ kg/m$^3$, $p_2 = 101155.8$ Pa, residuals of (1) to (4) below $10^{-9}$; the other root gives $p_2 = -6843.3$ Pa $< 0$ and is discarded.

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.h: Problem CL5: Turbojet on a Testbench: Exit State
chunks.x:
Official UC3M conservation-laws problem collection (Introduction to Fluid Mechanics). Part of Topic 3 - Conservation Laws. Related: integral balances, Reynolds transport theorem, formula sheet.
Method: each balance is written in full with the vanishing terms crossed out and the reason underneath; each surface integral is then evaluated surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class), and the wall terms are grouped (boxed) as the force on the body.

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.x:
The entrance and exit sections of the turboreactor sketched in the figure of CL5.pdf have areas $A_1$ and $A_2$. Besides the outer fixed frame, the machine has mobile parts in its interior that extract an amount of work $W$ per unit time from the fluid stream. The combined effects of chemical reaction in the combustion chamber and heat transfer through the walls give a heat transfer per unit time $Q$ to the fluid stream. The axial force on the turboreactor measured on the testbench is $\bar{F} = -F\,\bar{e}_x$. For given values of $W$, $Q$ and $F$ and assuming that at the entrance and exit sections the flow properties are uniform, obtain the values of the density $\rho_2$, pressure $p_2$ and velocity $v_2$ in terms of their values $p_1$, $\rho_1$ and $v_1$ at the entrance. (Handwritten addition: no gravity.)

*Statement figure (redrawn from CL5.pdf, p. 1): entrance $A_1$ ($v_1$, $p_1$, $\rho_1$), exit $A_2$ ($v_2$, $p_2$, $\rho_2$), rotor and heat sources $Q_r$, $Q_c$; the dashed control volume and its surfaces $\Sigma_1$ to $\Sigma_4$ belong to the official figure*

Source: CL5.pdf (page 1). Notes.pdf, Chapter 3: integral mass balance Eq. 3.10, integral momentum balance Eq. 3.35, integral total energy balance Eq. 3.46, force on a body Eq. 3.32.

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.x:
- Compressible flow; neglect gravity; uniform properties at inlet and outlet; steady on average (the rotating parts make the flow periodic inside, but there is no net accumulation).
- Perfect gas, $h = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p}{\rho}$, as in the class solution. Fuel mass flow neglected (not given), so the same mass flow crosses both sections.
- $\dot{W}$: work per unit time extracted from the fluid by the mobile parts; $\dot{Q}$: heat per unit time transferred to the fluid; $\bar{F} = -F\bar{e}_x$: force on the device measured on the testbench (fluid inside plus ambient air outside, at $p_a$).
- Data: $[\rho_1,\ p_1,\ \bar{v}_1 = v_1\bar{e}_x,\ A_1,\ A_2,\ F,\ \dot{W},\ \dot{Q}]$ and, introduced in the solution (not in the statement), the ambient pressure $p_a$ and the perfect-gas ratio $\gamma$. Unknowns: $[\rho_2,\ p_2,\ \bar{v}_2 = v_2\bar{e}_x]$.

| Symbol | Meaning | SI unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $A_1$, $A_2$ | entrance and exit areas | m$^2$ |
| $p_1$, $\rho_1$, $v_1$ | entrance state | Pa, kg/m$^3$, m/s |
| $p_2$, $\rho_2$, $v_2$ | exit state | Pa, kg/m$^3$, m/s |
| $F$ | thrust measured on the bench | N |
| $\dot{W}$, $\dot{Q}$ | power extracted and heat added | W |
| $\dot{m} = \rho_1v_1A_1$ | mass flow | kg/s |
| $p_a$, $\gamma$ | ambient pressure and specific-heat ratio (both introduced in the solution) | Pa, 1 |

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.h: Phase 2: Frames, Control Volume and Surfaces
chunks.x:
- Frame fixed to the testbench; $\bar{e}_x$ along the engine axis in the flow direction.
- Surfaces: $\Sigma_1$ (entrance, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_2$ (exit, $\bar{n} = +\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_w$ (fixed walls, $\bar{v} = \bar{v}_c = 0$) and $\Sigma_m$ (surface of the mobile parts, moving with them: $\bar{v} = \bar{v}_c \ne 0$). On $\Sigma_w$ and $\Sigma_m$, $(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n} = 0$.
- $\bar{n}$ is the outward normal of the control volume; $\bar{n}_{\text{in}} = -\bar{n}$ points into the fluid.

*Control volume of the solution (as in the class notes): $\Sigma_1$ (entrance, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_2$ (exit, $\bar{n} = +\bar{e}_x$), the fixed walls $\Sigma_w$ and the surface $\Sigma_m$ of the mobile parts. The official figure calls them $\Sigma_1$, $\Sigma_2$, $\Sigma_3$ and $\Sigma_4$*

Definitions written on the surfaces, as in class ($Q_R \equiv Q_c + Q_r$ is the volumetric heat release of Notes Eq. 3.46):

$$ \boxed{\,\bar{F} = \int_{\Sigma_m,\Sigma_w}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma - \int_{\Sigma_m,\Sigma_w}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma = -F\,\bar{e}_x\,} $$

$$ \boxed{\,\dot{Q} = \int_{\Sigma_w,\Sigma_m}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}_{\text{in}}\,d\sigma + \int_{V_c}Q_R\,dV\,} $$

$$ \boxed{\,\dot{W} = -\int_{\Sigma_m}p\,\bar{n}_{\text{in}}\cdot\bar{v}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_m}(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}_{\text{in}})\cdot\bar{v}\,d\sigma\,} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.h: Phase 2: Frames, Control Volume and Surfaces
chunks.x: Only $\Sigma_m$ enters $\dot{W}$: $\Sigma_w$ is a fixed surface and does no work. $\dot{W}$ is the power of the gas on the moving solid, so the power done on the gas there is $-\dot{W}$.

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.x:
**Mass (Notes Eq. 3.10)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{on average})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\,(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma = 0 $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\,(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $-\rho_1v_1A_1$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $+\rho_2v_2A_2$ |
| $\Sigma_m$ | $0$ ($\bar{v} = \bar{v}_c$) |
| $\Sigma_w$ | $0$ |

$$ \boxed{\,\rho_1v_1A_1 = \rho_2v_2A_2 = \dot{m}\,} \tag{1} $$

**Linear momentum (Notes Eq. 3.35)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{v}\,dV}}_{0} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect}} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.x:
| Surface | $\int\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma$ | $-\int(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $\rho_1v_1\bar{e}_x(-v_1)A_1 = -\dot{m}v_1\bar{e}_x$ | $(p_1 - p_a)A_1\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\rho_2v_2\bar{e}_x(v_2)A_2 = \dot{m}v_2\bar{e}_x$ | $-(p_2 - p_a)A_2\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ |
| **$\Sigma_m,\ \Sigma_w$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_m,\Sigma_w}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int_{\Sigma_m,\Sigma_w}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

Boxed $\Sigma_m$, $\Sigma_w$ terms: $-\bar{F} = F\bar{e}_x$ (uniform velocity vectors give no viscous stress on $\Sigma_1$, $\Sigma_2$).

$$ \boxed{\,\dot{m}\,(v_2 - v_1) = (p_1 - p_a)A_1 - (p_2 - p_a)A_2 + F\,} \tag{2} $$

**Total energy (Notes Eq. 3.46)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)dV}}_{0} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\left(e + \frac{v^2}{2}\right)[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\cdot\bar{v}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\cdot\bar{v}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect}} - \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{V_c}Q_R\,dV $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.x:
| Surface | $\int\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma$ | $-\int p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\cdot\bar{v}\,d\sigma$ | $-\int\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $-\dot{m}\left(e_1 + \tfrac{v_1^2}{2}\right)$ | $+p_1v_1A_1$ | $0$ | $0$ ($\nabla T = 0$) |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $+\dot{m}\left(e_2 + \tfrac{v_2^2}{2}\right)$ | $-p_2v_2A_2$ | $0$ | $0$ ($\nabla T = 0$) |
| **$\Sigma_m$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_m}p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int_{\Sigma_m}(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\cdot\bar{v}\,d\sigma$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_m}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| **$\Sigma_w$** (boxed) | $0$ | $0$ ($\bar{v} = 0$) | $0$ ($\bar{v} = 0$) | $-\int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

Boxed terms: the pressure and viscous work on $\Sigma_m$ add up to $-\dot{W}$; the conduction through $\Sigma_m$, $\Sigma_w$ plus the volume term $\int_{V_c}Q_R\,dV$ add up to $\dot{Q}$. Moving the pressure work on $\Sigma_1$, $\Sigma_2$ to the left gives $h = e + p/\rho$; with (1) and $h = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p}{\rho}$:

$$ \boxed{\,\dot{m}\left[\left(\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}\frac{p_2}{\rho_2} + \frac{v_2^2}{2}\right) - \left(\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}\frac{p_1}{\rho_1} + \frac{v_1^2}{2}\right)\right] = -\dot{W} + \dot{Q}\,} \tag{3} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.h: Phase 4: Interpretation, Limits and Dimensional Check
chunks.x:
- (2) is the thrust balance: thrust = change of momentum flux + pressure imbalance on the sections. For $p_1 = p_2 = p_a$, $F = \dot{m}(v_2 - v_1)$.
- (3): the stagnation enthalpy of the stream rises by the heat added and falls by the work extracted, per unit mass flow.
- Dimensions (SI): $[\dot{m}(v_2 - v_1)] = \text{N}$; $[(\dot{Q} - \dot{W})/\dot{m}] = \text{J/kg} = \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2 = [h] = [v^2]$.
- Numerical illustration (hypothetical data): $A_1 = 0.5$ m$^2$, $A_2 = 0.3$ m$^2$, $v_1 = 150$ m/s, $p_1 = 0.9\times10^5$ Pa, $\rho_1 = 1.1$ kg/m$^3$ ($M_1 = 0.443$), $p_a = 10^5$ Pa, $F = 30$ kN, $\dot{W} = 2$ MW, $\dot{Q} = 30$ MW, $\gamma = 1.4$: $\dot{m} = 82.5$ kg/s and the two roots of the extension below, $v_2 = 355.515$ m/s, $p_2 = 126817$ Pa, $\rho_2 = 0.77353$ kg/m$^3$ ($M_2 = 0.742$), and $v_2 = 597.263$ m/s, $p_2 = 60336$ Pa, $\rho_2 = 0.46043$ kg/m$^3$ ($M_2 = 1.39$); residuals of (1) to (3) below $10^{-6}$ in SI units.
- Agreement with the official and class solutions: the same equations (1), (2), (3) (CL5.pdf writes (2) as $F = \rho_1v_1A_1(v_2 - v_1) - (p_1 - p_a)A_1 + (p_2 - p_a)A_2$).

chunks.t: Problem - CL5 Turbojet on a Testbench
chunks.h: Phase 4: Interpretation, Limits and Dimensional Check
chunks.x:
Extension (beyond the official solution): explicit solution
With $K = p_aA_2 + F + (p_1 - p_a)A_1 + \dot{m}v_1$, (2) gives $p_2A_2 = K - \dot{m}v_2$ and, with (1), $p_2/\rho_2 = (K - \dot{m}v_2)v_2/\dot{m}$. Substituting into (3) and using $\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1} = -\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}$: $(\gamma + 1)v_2^2 - 2\gamma\frac{K}{\dot{m}}v_2 + 2(\gamma - 1)H_0 = 0$, with $H_0 = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p_1}{\rho_1} + \frac{v_1^2}{2} + \frac{\dot{Q} - \dot{W}}{\dot{m}}$. The two roots are a subsonic and a supersonic exit state; for a subsonic entrance with heat addition the physical one is the subsonic (smaller) root, since reaching the other would require passing through sonic conditions inside the engine, which this overall balance cannot describe. For $F = 0$, $\dot{Q} = \dot{W} = 0$ and $A_1 = A_2$ one root is $v_2 = v_1$ and the product of the roots is $2(\gamma - 1)H_0/(\gamma + 1)$, the Prandtl relation of a normal shock.

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.h: Problem CL6: Elbow Discharging a Vertical Jet: Velocity, Force and Heat
chunks.x:
Official UC3M conservation-laws problem collection (Introduction to Fluid Mechanics). Part of Topic 3 - Conservation Laws. Related: integral balances, Reynolds transport theorem, formula sheet.
Method: each balance is written in full with the vanishing terms crossed out and the reason underneath; each surface integral is then evaluated surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class), and the wall terms are grouped (boxed) as the force on the body.

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.x:
A liquid of density $\rho$ and specific heat $c$ flows through the elbow-shaped pipe shown in CL6.pdf, discharging to the atmosphere as a vertical jet through an outlet section of surface area $A_o$, different from the value $A_i$ at the inlet. Gravity is assumed to have a negligible effect on the fluid motion. Besides, uniform flow properties are assumed at the inlet and outlet sections, where readings from a thermometer give different values $T_i$ and $T_o$ for the temperature. The velocity at the outlet section is measured to be $v_o$ and a manometer is used to determine the value $p_i$ for the pressure at the inlet section. In terms of all of these quantities, determine:

- The value of the velocity at the inlet $v_i$.
- The two components of the force $(F_x, F_z)$ exerted on the pipe.
- The amount of heat $Q$ transferred per unit time to the liquid by heat conduction through the pipe walls.

*Statement figure (redrawn from CL6.pdf, p. 1): inlet section $A_i$ with $v_i$, $p_i$, $T_i$; outlet $A_o$ discharging a vertical jet $v_o$, $T_o$ into $p_a$; force components $F_x$, $F_z$ on the pipe and heat $Q$ through its walls*

Source: CL6.pdf (page 1), also solved in class (class notes, CL6). Notes.pdf, Chapter 3: integral mass balance Eq. 3.11, integral momentum balance Eq. 3.36, integral total energy balance Eq. 3.46.

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.x:
- Steady, incompressible liquid, $e = cT$; neglect $\bar{g}$; uniform properties at inlet and outlet (no viscous stresses or conduction across them).
- Free jet: $p = p_a$ over the outlet section. The outer face of the pipe is in contact with the ambient air at $p_a$, so the force on the pipe is computed with gauge pressure $p - p_a$.
- Geometry (figure): the liquid enters horizontally along $+\bar{e}_x$ and leaves as a vertical jet along $-\bar{e}_z$ ($\bar{e}_z$ upwards).
- Data: $[\rho,\ c,\ A_i,\ A_o,\ v_o,\ p_i,\ p_a,\ T_i,\ T_o]$. Unknowns: $[v_i,\ F_x,\ F_z,\ \dot{Q}]$.

| Symbol | Meaning | SI unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $A_i$, $A_o$ | inlet and outlet areas | m$^2$ |
| $v_i$, $v_o$ | inlet and outlet velocities | m/s |
| $p_i$, $p_a$ | inlet and ambient pressures | Pa |
| $T_i$, $T_o$ | inlet and outlet temperatures | K |
| $c$ | specific heat of the liquid | J/(kg$\cdot$K) |
| $\dot{Q}$ | heat per unit time into the liquid | W |
| $\rho$ | liquid density | kg/m$^3$ |

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.h: Phase 2: Frames, Control Volume and Surfaces
chunks.x:
- Frame fixed to the pipe, $\bar{e}_x$ horizontal (inlet flow direction), $\bar{e}_z$ vertical upwards. Fixed control volume: the liquid inside the pipe, $\bar{v}_c = 0$.
- Surfaces: $\Sigma_i$ (inlet, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$, $\bar{v} = v_i\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_o$ (outlet, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_z$, $\bar{v} = -v_o\bar{e}_z$), $\Sigma_w$ (pipe wall, $\bar{v} = 0$).

*Control volume of the solution (as in the class notes): the liquid inside the pipe, with $\Sigma_i$ (inlet, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_o$ (outlet, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_z$) and the wall $\Sigma_w$, where the force and the heat are collected*

Force of the liquid and the ambient air on the pipe, and heat through the walls, written on $\Sigma_w$:

$$ \boxed{\,\bar{F} = F_x\bar{e}_x + F_z\bar{e}_z = \int_{\Sigma_w}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma - \int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma\,} $$

$$ \boxed{\,\dot{Q} = -\int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma\,} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.x:
**Mass (Notes Eq. 3.11)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\,(\bar{v} - \underbrace{\cancel{\bar{v}_c}}_{0})\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma = 0 $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_i$ | $\rho\,v_i\bar{e}_x\cdot(-\bar{e}_x)A_i = -\rho v_iA_i$ |
| $\Sigma_o$ | $\rho\,(-v_o\bar{e}_z)\cdot(-\bar{e}_z)A_o = +\rho v_oA_o$ |
| $\Sigma_w$ | $0$ |

$$ \boxed{\,v_i = \frac{A_o}{A_i}\,v_o\,},\qquad \dot{m} = \rho v_iA_i = \rho v_oA_o \tag{1} $$

**Linear momentum (Notes Eq. 3.36)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{v}\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \underbrace{\cancel{\bar{v}_c}}_{0})\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect } \bar{g}} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.x:
| Surface | $\int\rho\bar{v}\,(\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_i$ | $\rho v_i\bar{e}_x\,(-v_i)A_i = -\rho v_i^2A_i\,\bar{e}_x$ | $-(p_i - p_a)(-\bar{e}_x)A_i = (p_i - p_a)A_i\,\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_o$ | $\rho(-v_o\bar{e}_z)\,(v_o)A_o = -\rho v_o^2A_o\,\bar{e}_z$ | $0$ (free jet) | $0$ |
| **$\Sigma_w$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_w}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

Boxed $\Sigma_w$ terms: $-\bar{F}$.

$$ -\rho v_i^2A_i\,\bar{e}_x - \rho v_o^2A_o\,\bar{e}_z = (p_i - p_a)A_i\,\bar{e}_x - \bar{F} \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,F_x = \left[\rho v_i^2 + (p_i - p_a)\right]A_i,\qquad F_z = \rho v_o^2A_o\,} \tag{2} $$

**Total energy (Notes Eq. 3.46; $Q_R \equiv Q_c + Q_r$ is the volumetric heat release)**

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.x:
$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\left(e + \frac{v^2}{2}\right)[(\bar{v} - \underbrace{\cancel{\bar{v}_c}}_{0})\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\cdot\bar{v}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect } \bar{g}} - \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}Q_R\,dV}}_{0} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)(\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_i$ | $-\dot{m}\left(cT_i + \tfrac{v_i^2}{2}\right)$ | $+p_iv_iA_i$ | $0$ | $0$ (uniform $T$) |
| $\Sigma_o$ | $+\dot{m}\left(cT_o + \tfrac{v_o^2}{2}\right)$ | $-p_av_oA_o$ | $0$ | $0$ (uniform $T$) |
| **$\Sigma_w$** (boxed) | $0$ | $0$ ($\bar{v} = 0$) | $0$ ($\bar{v} = 0$) | $-\int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

Boxed $\Sigma_w$ term: $\dot{Q}$. Using (1), $p_iv_iA_i - p_av_oA_o = (p_i - p_a)\,v_oA_o$.

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.x: $$ \dot{m}\left[c(T_o - T_i) + \frac{v_o^2 - v_i^2}{2}\right] = (p_i - p_a)\,v_oA_o + \dot{Q} \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,\dot{Q} = \rho v_oA_o\left[c(T_o - T_i) + \frac{v_o^2 - v_i^2}{2}\right] + (p_a - p_i)\,v_oA_o\,} \tag{3} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL6 Elbow with Vertical Jet
chunks.h: Phase 4: Interpretation, Limits and Dimensional Check
chunks.x:
- $F_x > 0$: the pipe is pushed along the incoming flow by the momentum flux and the gauge pressure at the inlet. $F_z > 0$: the jet leaves downwards, so the pipe is pushed upwards.
- (3) splits the heat into the rise of internal energy, the change of kinetic energy and the flow work. If no heat were exchanged and there were no losses, (3) with $\dot{Q} = 0$ and $T_o = T_i$ would reduce to Bernoulli's equation $p_i + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_i^2 = p_a + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_o^2$.
- Dimensions (SI): $[\rho v_i^2A_i] = [(p_i - p_a)A_i] = \text{N}$; $[\rho v_oA_o\,c\,\Delta T] = (\text{kg/s})(\text{J/(kg K)})\,\text{K} = \text{W}$; $[(p_a - p_i)v_oA_o] = \text{Pa}\cdot\text{m}^3/\text{s} = \text{W}$.
- Numerical illustration (hypothetical data): water, $c = 4186$ J/(kg K), $A_i = 0.01$ m$^2$, $A_o = 0.004$ m$^2$, $v_o = 6$ m/s, $p_i = 1.6\times10^5$ Pa, $p_a = 101325$ Pa, $T_o - T_i = 0.5$ K give $v_i = 2.4$ m/s, $F_x = 644.35$ N, $F_z = 144$ N and $\dot{Q} = 49187$ W.
- Agreement with the official and class solutions: (1), (2) and (3) are the results of CL6.pdf (which labels the vertical axis $y$: $F_y = \rho v_o^2A_o$) and of the class notes.

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.h: Problem CL7: Industrial Dryer: Velocities, Force, Power and Torque
chunks.x:
Official UC3M conservation-laws problem collection (Introduction to Fluid Mechanics). Part of Topic 3 - Conservation Laws. Related: integral balances, Reynolds transport theorem, formula sheet.
Method: each balance is written in full with the vanishing terms crossed out and the reason underneath; each surface integral is then evaluated surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class), and the wall terms are grouped (boxed) as the force on the body.

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.x:
The axisymmetric industrial dryer of the figure in CL7.pdf is designed to provide a steady hot jet of radius $R$, mass flux $G$, and temperature $T_s$. Air enters the dryer from the ambient, at temperature and pressure $T_a$ and $p_a$, through a radial inlet of surface $A$. Inside the dryer there exists an electric resistance that releases an amount of heat $Q$ per unit time, as well as a fan of power $W$ (work per unit time). Because of the presence of the fan, the air velocity at the exit has both azimuthal and axial components, $v_\theta$ and $v_z$, such that $v_\theta/v_z = \tan(\beta)$. In the analysis, assume that the fan and the inner walls of the dryer are thermally insulated, that the air behaves as an ideal gas with constant $R_g$ and specific heat at constant pressure $c_p$, that gravity has a negligible effect on the fluid motion, and that the flow properties are uniform at the inlet and outlet sections. For given values of $G$, $T_s$, $T_a$, $p_a$, $A$, $R$, $R_g$, $c_p$ and $\tan(\beta)$, determine:

- The velocity at the entrance section $v_r$ as well as the two velocity components at the exit $v_\theta$ and $v_z$.
- The force acting on the dryer, indicating clearly its magnitude and direction.
- The total power required to run the dryer $Q + W$.
- The torque acting on the dryer.

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.x:
*Statement figure (CL7.pdf, p. 1, cropped): radial inlet $A$ ($v_r$, $\rho_a$), resistance and fan, exit of diameter $2R$ with $v_z$ and $v_\theta$; the surface names and notes are handwritten on the official sheet*

Source: CL7.pdf (page 1). Notes.pdf, Chapter 3: integral mass balance Eq. 3.11, integral momentum balance Eq. 3.35, integral angular momentum balance Eq. 3.38, integral total energy balance Eq. 3.46.

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.x:
- Steady (on average) axisymmetric flow; ideal gas $p = \rho R_gT$, so $h = e + p/\rho = c_pT$; neglect $\bar{g}$; uniform properties at inlet and outlet.
- Inlet: air taken from the ambient, with $p = p_a$, $T = T_a$, $\rho_a = p_a/(R_gT_a)$ and radial velocity $v_r$ pointing inwards (as in the official solution). Exit: free jet, $p = p_a$, $T = T_s$, $\rho_s = p_a/(R_gT_s)$, velocity $v_z\bar{e}_z + v_\theta\bar{e}_\theta$ uniform over the disc of radius $R$.
- $G$ is the mass flow rate of the jet (kg/s), as used in the official solution ($G = \rho_av_rA$). Fan and inner walls insulated; the resistance releases $\dot{Q}$; the fan delivers the power $\dot{W}$ to the air.
- Data: $[G,\ T_s,\ T_a,\ p_a,\ A,\ R,\ R_g,\ c_p,\ \tan\beta]$. Unknowns: $[v_r,\ v_z,\ v_\theta,\ \bar{F},\ \dot{Q} + \dot{W},\ \bar{M}]$.

| Symbol | Meaning | SI unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $G$ | mass flow rate | kg/s |
| $A$, $R$ | inlet area, jet radius | m$^2$, m |
| $v_r$, $v_z$, $v_\theta$ | inlet and exit velocities | m/s |
| $R_g$, $c_p$ | gas constant, specific heat | J/(kg$\cdot$K) |
| $\bar{F}$, $\bar{M}$ | force and torque on the dryer | N, N$\cdot$m |
| $T_s$, $T_a$, $p_a$ | exit and ambient temperatures, ambient pressure | K, K, Pa |
| $\tan\beta = v_\theta/v_z$ | swirl ratio at the exit | 1 |

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.h: Phase 2: Frames, Control Volume and Surfaces
chunks.x:
- Frame fixed to the dryer; cylindrical basis $(\bar{e}_r, \bar{e}_\theta, \bar{e}_z)$ with $\bar{e}_z$ along the axis in the jet direction; origin on the axis. By axisymmetry the integrals of the unit vectors over a full turn vanish: with two fixed unit vectors $\bar{e}_x$, $\bar{e}_y$ normal to the axis ($\bar{e}_x\wedge\bar{e}_y = \bar{e}_z$), $\bar{e}_r = \cos\theta\,\bar{e}_x + \sin\theta\,\bar{e}_y$ and $\bar{e}_\theta = -\sin\theta\,\bar{e}_x + \cos\theta\,\bar{e}_y$, so $\int_0^{2\pi}\bar{e}_r\,d\theta = [\sin\theta]_0^{2\pi}\,\bar{e}_x + [-\cos\theta]_0^{2\pi}\,\bar{e}_y = \bar{0}$ and $\int_0^{2\pi}\bar{e}_\theta\,d\theta = [\cos\theta]_0^{2\pi}\,\bar{e}_x + [\sin\theta]_0^{2\pi}\,\bar{e}_y = \bar{0}$.
- Surfaces: $\Sigma_1$ (radial inlet, area $A$, $\bar{n} = \bar{e}_r$, $\bar{v} = -v_r\bar{e}_r$), $\Sigma_2$ (exit disc, $\bar{n} = \bar{e}_z$), $\Sigma_w$ (fixed casing and resistance, $\bar{v} = 0$) and $\Sigma_m$ (fan blades, $\bar{v} = \bar{v}_c$).

*Control volume of the solution (schematic axial section): $\Sigma_1$ (radial inlet of area $A$, $\bar{n} = \bar{e}_r$, $\bar{v} = -v_r\bar{e}_r$), $\Sigma_2$ (exit disc of radius $R$, $\bar{n} = \bar{e}_z$), $\Sigma_w$ (fixed casing and resistance) and $\Sigma_m$ (fan blades, dashed around them); the heat $Q$ is released by the resistance*

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.h: Phase 2: Frames, Control Volume and Surfaces
chunks.x:
Force and torque of the air (inside, and ambient outside) on the dryer, and the heat and work exchanged:

$$ \boxed{\,\bar{F} = \int_{\Sigma_w,\Sigma_m}\left[(p - p_a)\,\bar{n} - \bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\right]d\sigma\,} $$

$$ \boxed{\,\bar{M} = \int_{\Sigma_w,\Sigma_m}\bar{x}\wedge\left[(p - p_a)\,\bar{n} - \bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\right]d\sigma\,} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.x:
**Mass (Notes Eq. 3.11)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\,(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma = 0 $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\,(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $\rho_a(-v_r)A = -\rho_av_rA$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\rho_sv_z\pi R^2$ |
| $\Sigma_w,\ \Sigma_m$ | $0$ |

$$ G = \frac{p_a}{R_gT_a}\,v_rA = \frac{p_a}{R_gT_s}\,v_z\pi R^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,v_r = \frac{GR_gT_a}{p_aA},\qquad v_z = \frac{GR_gT_s}{p_a\pi R^2},\qquad v_\theta = v_z\tan\beta\,} \tag{1} $$

**Linear momentum (Notes Eq. 3.35)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{v}\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect } \bar{g}} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.x:
| Surface | $\int\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma$ | $-\int(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $\rho_av_r^2\int_{\Sigma_1}\bar{e}_r\,d\sigma = 0$ (axisymmetric) | $0$ ($p = p_a$) | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\rho_sv_z\int_{\Sigma_2}(v_z\bar{e}_z + v_\theta\bar{e}_\theta)\,d\sigma = \rho_sv_z^2\pi R^2\,\bar{e}_z$ | $0$ (free jet) | $0$ |
| **$\Sigma_w,\ \Sigma_m$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

Boxed terms: $-\bar{F}$. On $\Sigma_2$, $\int_{\Sigma_2}\bar{e}_\theta\,d\sigma = 0$, so the swirl gives no force.

$$ \rho_sv_z^2\pi R^2\,\bar{e}_z = -\bar{F} \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,\bar{F} = -\frac{p_a}{R_gT_s}\,v_z^2\,\pi R^2\,\bar{e}_z = -G\,v_z\,\bar{e}_z\,} \tag{2} $$

**Total energy (Notes Eq. 3.46; $Q_R \equiv Q_c + Q_r$ is the volumetric heat release)**

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.x:
$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\left(e + \frac{v^2}{2}\right)[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\cdot\bar{v}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect } \bar{g}} - \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}Q_R\,dV}}_{0} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)(\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $-G\left(e_a + \tfrac{v_r^2}{2}\right)$ | $+p_av_rA$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $+G\left(e_s + \tfrac{v_\theta^2 + v_z^2}{2}\right)$ | $-p_av_z\pi R^2$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| **$\Sigma_m$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_m}p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int_{\Sigma_m}\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $0$ (insulated) |
| **$\Sigma_w$** (boxed) | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.x:
Boxed terms: the work on $\Sigma_m$ is the fan power $\dot{W}$; the heat through $\Sigma_w$ (only the resistance, the walls are insulated) is $\dot{Q}$. With $p_av_rA = G\,p_a/\rho_a$ and $p_av_z\pi R^2 = G\,p_a/\rho_s$, $e + p/\rho = c_pT$:

$$ \boxed{\,\dot{Q} + \dot{W} = G\left[\left(c_pT_s + \frac{v_\theta^2 + v_z^2}{2}\right) - \left(c_pT_a + \frac{v_r^2}{2}\right)\right]\,} \tag{3} $$

**Angular momentum about the origin, z component (Notes Eq. 3.38)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\,\bar{x}\wedge\bar{v}\,dV}}_{0} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\,(\bar{x}\wedge\bar{v})[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{x}\wedge(p - p_a)\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{x}\wedge(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\,(\bar{x}\wedge\bar{v})_z\,[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma$ | $\text{pressure and viscous moments}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $0$ ($\bar{x}\wedge(-v_r\bar{e}_r) = -zv_r\,\bar{e}_\theta$, no $z$ component) | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\int_0^R\rho_sv_z\,(rv_\theta)\,2\pi r\,dr = \rho_sv_zv_\theta\,\frac{2\pi R^3}{3}$ | $0$ |
| **$\Sigma_w,\ \Sigma_m$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\bar{M}\cdot\bar{e}_z$ |

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.x:
On $\Sigma_2$, $\bar{x} = r\bar{e}_r + z_2\bar{e}_z$ and $\bar{x}\wedge(v_z\bar{e}_z + v_\theta\bar{e}_\theta) = -rv_z\bar{e}_\theta + rv_\theta\bar{e}_z - z_2v_\theta\bar{e}_r$; only $rv_\theta\bar{e}_z$ survives the integral. The antiderivative of $r^2$ is $r^3/3$, and Barrow's rule between $0$ and $R$ gives $R^3/3$.

$$ \boxed{\,\bar{M} = -\rho_sv_zv_\theta\,\frac{2\pi R^3}{3}\,\bar{e}_z = -\frac{2}{3}\,R\,G\,v_\theta\,\bar{e}_z\,} \tag{4} $$

Erratum in the official solution (slip in the boxed result)
CL7.pdf writes the momentum balance as $\frac{p_a}{R_gT_s}v_z^2\pi R^2\bar{e}_z = -\bar{F}$ but boxes $\bar{F} = -\frac{p_a}{R_gT_s}v_z^2\bar{e}_z$, without the area $\pi R^2$. That expression has units of pressure, not force; the correct result is (2).

chunks.t: Problem - CL7 Industrial Dryer
chunks.h: Phase 4: Interpretation, Limits and Dimensional Check
chunks.x:
- The radial inflow gives no net momentum (axisymmetry), so the force is the reaction to the jet: magnitude $Gv_z$, direction $-\bar{e}_z$ (opposite to the jet).
- The swirl gives no force but gives a torque: the fan sets the air rotating, and the air reacts on the dryer with $\bar{M}$ opposite to the swirl. For $\beta = 0$, $v_\theta = 0$ and $\bar{M} = 0$.
- (3): the electric and mechanical power go into heating the air from $T_a$ to $T_s$ and into its kinetic energy.
- Dimensions (SI): $[Gv_z] = \text{N}$; $[RGv_\theta] = \text{m}\cdot(\text{kg/s})(\text{m/s}) = \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$; $[Gc_pT] = \text{W}$.
- Numerical illustration (hypothetical data): $G = 0.5$ kg/s, $T_s = 350$ K, $T_a = 293$ K, $p_a = 101325$ Pa, $A = 0.05$ m$^2$, $R = 0.05$ m, $R_g = 287$ J/(kg K), $c_p = 1005$ J/(kg K), $\tan\beta = 0.5$ give $v_r = 8.2991$ m/s, $v_z = 63.112$ m/s, $v_\theta = 31.556$ m/s, $|\bar{F}| = 31.556$ N, $\dot{Q} + \dot{W} = 29870$ W and $|\bar{M}| = 0.52594$ N$\cdot$m (a midpoint quadrature of the torque integral gives the same value).

chunks.t: Problem - CL8 Jet on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.h: Problem CL8: Jet Impinging on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.x:
Official UC3M conservation-laws problem collection (Introduction to Fluid Mechanics). Part of Topic 3 - Conservation Laws. Related: integral balances, Reynolds transport theorem, formula sheet.
Method: each balance is written in full with the vanishing terms crossed out and the reason underneath; each surface integral is then evaluated surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class), and the wall terms are grouped (boxed) as the force on the body.

chunks.t: Problem - CL8 Jet on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.x:
A circular water jet of diameter $D_j$ and velocity $V_j$ impinges perpendicularly to a wall, where there exists an orifice centered at the jet axis, as shown in the figure of CL8.pdf, so that part of the water flows through the orifice and part is deflected to flow next to the wall. Assuming that the flow velocity is sufficiently large for the effects of viscosity and gravity to be negligible:

- Determine the values of the velocities $V_s$ and $V_r$ for the secondary jet that emerges from the orifice and for the radial wall jet.
- Obtain the thickness $h(r)$ of the radial wall jet.
- Compute the force that the jet exerts on the wall as a function of $\rho$, $V_j$, $D_j$ and $D_s$.

*Statement figure (redrawn from CL8.pdf, p. 1, axial section): incoming jet $D_j$, $V_j$; orifice of diameter $D_s$ with the secondary jet $V_s$; radial wall jet $V_r$ of thickness $h(r)$; ambient pressure $p_a$ on both sides of the wall*

Source: CL8.pdf (page 1). Notes.pdf: Bernoulli's equation Eq. 4.17 (Chapter 4), integral mass balance Eq. 3.11, integral momentum balance Eq. 3.36.

chunks.t: Problem - CL8 Jet on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.x:
- Steady, incompressible, frictionless (viscosity negligible); neglect $\bar{g}$ (buoyancy-free).
- Free jets surrounded by the ambient air at $p_a$. In each jet away from the wall the streamlines are straight and parallel (aligned), so the pressure does not vary across them: $p = p_a$ inside the incoming jet, the secondary jet and the wall jet (official solution).
- Data: $[\rho,\ V_j,\ D_j,\ D_s]$. Unknowns: $[V_s,\ V_r,\ h(r),\ \bar{F}_w]$.

| Symbol | Meaning | SI unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $V_j$, $D_j$ | velocity and diameter of the jet | m/s, m |
| $V_s$, $D_s$ | secondary jet velocity, orifice diameter | m/s, m |
| $V_r$, $h(r)$ | wall-jet velocity and thickness | m/s, m |
| $\bar{F}_w$ | force of the jet on the wall | N |

chunks.t: Problem - CL8 Jet on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.h: Phase 2: Frames, Control Volume and Surfaces
chunks.x:
- Frame fixed to the wall; $\bar{e}_x$ along the jet axis (towards the wall); cylindrical coordinate $r$ on the wall, with two fixed unit vectors $\bar{e}_y$, $\bar{e}_z$ normal to $\bar{e}_x$, $\bar{e}_r = \cos\theta\,\bar{e}_y + \sin\theta\,\bar{e}_z$ and $\int_0^{2\pi}\bar{e}_r\,d\theta = [\sin\theta]_0^{2\pi}\,\bar{e}_y + [-\cos\theta]_0^{2\pi}\,\bar{e}_z = \bar{0}$.
- Fixed control volume around the water: $\Sigma_j$ (section of the incoming jet, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_s$ (section of the secondary jet beyond the orifice, $\bar{n} = +\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_r$ (cylinder of radius $r$ across the wall jet, $\bar{n} = \bar{e}_r$, height $h$), $\Sigma_a$ (free surfaces, $p = p_a$, $\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n} = 0$) and $\Sigma_w$ (wetted wall).

*Control volume of the solution: $\Sigma_j$ (incoming jet, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_s$ (secondary jet, $\bar{n} = +\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_r$ (cylinder of radius $r$ across the wall jet, $\bar{n} = \bar{e}_r$; its two traces in this section), the free surfaces $\Sigma_a$ at $p_a$ and the wetted wall $\Sigma_w$; $\bar{F}_w$ is the force on the wall*

Force of the water (and of the ambient air on the dry side) on the wall:

$$ \boxed{\,\bar{F}_w = \int_{\Sigma_w}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma - \int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma\,} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL8 Jet on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.x:
Why this tool: for steady, frictionless, incompressible flow without mass forces, $p + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho|\bar{v}|^2$ is constant along a streamline (Notes Eq. 4.17 with $U = 0$, as used in the official solution). Take a streamline from the incoming jet to the wall jet, and another one to the secondary jet; at both ends $p = p_a$:

$$ p_a + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V_j^2 = p_a + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V_r^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,V_r = V_j\,},\qquad p_a + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V_j^2 = p_a + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V_s^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,V_s = V_j\,} \tag{1} $$

**Mass (Notes Eq. 3.11)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\,(\bar{v} - \underbrace{\cancel{\bar{v}_c}}_{0})\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma = 0 $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_j$ | $-\rho V_j\frac{\pi D_j^2}{4}$ |
| $\Sigma_s$ | $+\rho V_s\frac{\pi D_s^2}{4}$ |
| $\Sigma_r$ | $+\rho V_r\,2\pi r\,h$ |
| $\Sigma_a,\ \Sigma_w$ | $0$ |

With (1), $V_s = V_r = V_j$ and the velocity cancels.

$$ -\frac{\pi D_j^2}{4} + \frac{\pi D_s^2}{4} + 2\pi rh = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,h(r) = \frac{D_j^2 - D_s^2}{8\,r}\,} \tag{2} $$

**Linear momentum (Notes Eq. 3.36)**

chunks.t: Problem - CL8 Jet on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.x:
$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{v}\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \underbrace{\cancel{\bar{v}_c}}_{0})\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect } \bar{g}} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\bar{v}\,(\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_j$ | $\rho V_j\bar{e}_x(-V_j)\frac{\pi D_j^2}{4} = -\rho V_j^2\frac{\pi D_j^2}{4}\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ ($p = p_a$) | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_s$ | $+\rho V_s^2\frac{\pi D_s^2}{4}\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ ($p = p_a$) | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_r$ | $\rho V_r^2h\,r\int_0^{2\pi}\bar{e}_r\,d\theta = 0$ | $0$ ($p = p_a$) | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_a$ | $0$ | $0$ ($p = p_a$) | $0$ |
| **$\Sigma_w$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_w}(p - p_a)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int_{\Sigma_w}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

Boxed $\Sigma_w$ terms: $-\bar{F}_w$. With (1), $V_s = V_j$.

chunks.t: Problem - CL8 Jet on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.x: $$ \left(\rho V_j^2\frac{\pi D_s^2}{4} - \rho V_j^2\frac{\pi D_j^2}{4}\right)\bar{e}_x = -\bar{F}_w \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,\bar{F}_w = \rho V_j^2\,\frac{\pi}{4}\left(D_j^2 - D_s^2\right)\bar{e}_x\,} \tag{3} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL8 Jet on a Wall with an Orifice
chunks.h: Phase 4: Interpretation, Limits and Dimensional Check
chunks.x:
- Only the part of the jet stopped by the wall (the annulus between $D_s$ and $D_j$) pushes on it; the secondary jet keeps its momentum. For $D_s \to 0$, $\bar{F}_w \to \rho V_j^2\pi D_j^2/4$, the force of a jet on a flat plate; for $D_s \to D_j$ the jet passes through and $\bar{F}_w \to 0$, $h \to 0$.
- $h \propto 1/r$: the wall jet thins as it spreads, keeping the flow rate $2\pi rhV_j$ constant.
- Dimensions (SI): $[h] = \text{m}^2/\text{m} = \text{m}$; $[\rho V_j^2D^2] = \text{N}$.
- Numerical illustration (hypothetical data): $\rho = 1000$ kg/m$^3$, $V_j = 10$ m/s, $D_j = 0.05$ m, $D_s = 0.02$ m give $|\bar{F}_w| = 164.93$ N and $h(0.1\ \text{m}) = 2.625$ mm.
- Agreement with the official solution: CL8.pdf obtains (1), (2) and (3).

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.h: Problem CL9: Submarine Propulsion Device: Thrust from the Propeller Power
chunks.x:
Official UC3M conservation-laws problem collection (Introduction to Fluid Mechanics). Part of Topic 3 - Conservation Laws. Related: integral balances, Reynolds transport theorem, formula sheet.
Method: each balance is written in full with the vanishing terms crossed out and the reason underneath; each surface integral is then evaluated surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class), and the wall terms are grouped (boxed) as the force on the body.

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x: The submarine propulsion device schematically represented in the figure of CL9.pdf consists of a nozzle, with inlet and outlet cross-section area $A_e$ and $A_s$, and a propeller (printed as 'fan', corrected by hand to 'propeller') located inside, which imparts a rate of work per unit time (power) $\dot{W}$ to the circulating water stream, whose density and viscosity are $\rho$ and $\mu$, respectively. To determine the thrust $T$ produced when the submarine is at rest and at sufficient depth for gravity to have a negligible effect, please follow these steps:

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x:
- By application of the continuity equation determine a relationship between the uniform velocities $U_e$ and $U_s$ at the inlet and outlet sections.
- Use the momentum conservation equation to obtain an expression for the thrust (axial force) that the fluid exerts on the propulsion device as a function of the flow conditions at the inlet and outlet. Assume that the pressure surrounding the device is equal to the ambient pressure $p_\infty$.
- Assuming that the flow upstream from the entrance is steady and inviscid, use Bernoulli's equation along a given streamline to find a relationship between the flow conditions in the stagnant atmosphere (1) and at the entrance $e$.
- Use the energy equation to relate the work per unit time $\dot{W}$ with the different fluid variables appearing in the problem. Assume that the variation of internal energy between the inlet and outlet sections is negligible ($e_e = e_s$) and that all of the device walls, including those of the fan, are thermally insulated.
- Combine the above equations to show that the thrust can be expressed in the form $T/(\rho^{1/3}\dot{W}^{2/3}A_s^{1/3}) = f(A_e/A_s)$, obtaining the function $f$.

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x:
*Statement figure (redrawn from CL9.pdf, p. 1): nozzle of inlet area $A_e$ ($U_e$, $p_e$) and outlet area $A_s$ ($U_s$, $p_s$); propeller supplying the power $\dot{W}$; thrust $T$; the streamline from the still water at point 1 ($p_\infty$) to the inlet $e$*

Source: CL9.pdf (page 1). Notes.pdf: integral mass balance Eq. 3.11, integral momentum balance Eq. 3.35, integral total energy balance Eq. 3.46, Bernoulli's equation Eq. 4.17.

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x:
- Steady (on average), incompressible water; gravity negligible at depth (it is absorbed in the reduced pressure $p + \rho gz$, as the official solution notes); uniform properties at $e$ and $s$.
- Viscous stresses negligible on the sections ($\rho UD/\mu \gg 1$); the exit jet discharges at the ambient pressure, $p_s = p_\infty$; walls and propeller insulated; $e_e = e_s$.
- Data: $[\rho,\ A_e,\ A_s,\ \dot{W},\ p_\infty]$. Unknowns: $[U_e,\ U_s,\ p_e,\ T]$.

| Symbol | Meaning | SI unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $A_e$, $A_s$ | inlet and outlet areas | m$^2$ |
| $U_e$, $U_s$ | inlet and outlet velocities | m/s |
| $p_e$, $p_\infty$ | inlet and ambient pressures | Pa |
| $\dot{W}$ | power given by the propeller to the water | W |
| $T$ | thrust | N |
| $\rho$ | water density | kg/m$^3$ |

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.h: Phase 2: Frames, Control Volume and Surfaces
chunks.x:
- Frame fixed to the submarine (at rest), $\bar{e}_x$ along the axis in the direction of the exit jet. The thrust pushes the device towards $-\bar{e}_x$: $\bar{F} = -T\bar{e}_x$ is the force of the water (inside and outside, at $p_\infty$) on the device.
- Surfaces: $\Sigma_e$ (inlet, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_s$ (outlet, $\bar{n} = +\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_w$ (nozzle walls, fixed) and $\Sigma_p$ (propeller, moving).

*Control volume of the solution: $\Sigma_e$ (inlet, $\bar{n} = -\bar{e}_x$), $\Sigma_s$ (outlet, $\bar{n} = +\bar{e}_x$), the fixed nozzle walls $\Sigma_w$ and the moving propeller $\Sigma_p$ (dashed around it); the force of the water on the device is $\bar{F} = -T\bar{e}_x$*

$$ \boxed{\,\bar{F} = -T\,\bar{e}_x = \int_{\Sigma_w,\Sigma_p}\left[(p - p_\infty)\,\bar{n} - \bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\right]d\sigma\,} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x:
**(1) Mass (Notes Eq. 3.11)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\,(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma = 0 $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

| Surface | $\int\rho\,(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_e$ | $-\rho U_eA_e$ |
| $\Sigma_s$ | $+\rho U_sA_s$ |
| $\Sigma_w,\ \Sigma_p$ | $0$ |

$$ \boxed{\,U_eA_e = U_sA_s\,} \tag{1} $$

**(2) Linear momentum (Notes Eq. 3.35)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{v}\,dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}(p - p_\infty)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect } \bar{g}} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x:
| Surface | $\int\rho\bar{v}\,[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma$ | $-\int(p - p_\infty)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_e$ | $-\rho U_e^2A_e\,\bar{e}_x$ | $(p_e - p_\infty)A_e\,\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_s$ | $+\rho U_s^2A_s\,\bar{e}_x$ | $0$ ($p_s = p_\infty$) | $0$ |
| **$\Sigma_w,\ \Sigma_p$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int(p - p_\infty)\,\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |

Boxed terms: $-\bar{F} = T\bar{e}_x$. With (1), $\rho U_s^2A_s - \rho U_e^2A_e = \rho U_eA_e(U_s - U_e)$.

$$ \rho U_eA_e(U_s - U_e) = (p_e - p_\infty)A_e + T \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,T = \rho U_eA_e\,(U_s - U_e) - (p_e - p_\infty)A_e\,} \tag{2} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x:
Steady inviscid flow from the stagnant water far ahead (1), where $v = 0$ and $p = p_\infty$, to the inlet $e$ (Notes Eq. 4.17 with the reduced pressure):

$$ p_\infty = p_e + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho U_e^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,p_e - p_\infty = -\tfrac{1}{2}\rho U_e^2\,} \tag{3} $$

**(4) Total energy (Notes Eq. 3.46; $Q_R \equiv Q_c + Q_r$ is the volumetric heat release)**

$$ \underbrace{\cancel{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_c}\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)dV}}_{0\ (\text{steady})} + \int_{\Sigma_c}\rho\left(e + \frac{v^2}{2}\right)[(\bar{v} - \bar{v}_c)\cdot\bar{n}]\,d\sigma = -\int_{\Sigma_c}p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}\rho\bar{g}\cdot\bar{v}\,dV}}_{\text{neglect } \bar{g}} - \int_{\Sigma_c}\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma + \underbrace{\cancel{\int_{V_c}Q_R\,dV}}_{0} $$

Each surface integral, surface by surface (the vertical line drawn under each integral in class):

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x:
| Surface | $\int\rho\left(e + \tfrac{v^2}{2}\right)(\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $-\int\bar{q}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_e$ | $-\rho U_eA_e\left(e_e + \tfrac{U_e^2}{2}\right)$ | $+p_eU_eA_e$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $\Sigma_s$ | $+\rho U_sA_s\left(e_s + \tfrac{U_s^2}{2}\right)$ | $-p_\infty U_sA_s$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| **$\Sigma_p$** (boxed) | $0$ | $-\int_{\Sigma_p}p\,\bar{v}\cdot\bar{n}\,d\sigma$ | $\int_{\Sigma_p}\bar{v}\cdot(\bar{\bar{\tau}}'\cdot\bar{n})\,d\sigma$ | $0$ (insulated) |
| $\Sigma_w$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ (insulated) |

Boxed $\Sigma_p$ terms: the propeller power $\dot{W}$. With $e_e = e_s$, $\rho U_eA_e = \rho U_sA_s = \dot{m}$ and (3):

$$ \dot{W} = \dot{m}\left[\frac{p_\infty - p_e}{\rho} + \frac{U_s^2 - U_e^2}{2}\right] = \dot{m}\left[\frac{U_e^2}{2} + \frac{U_s^2 - U_e^2}{2}\right] \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\,\dot{W} = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho A_sU_s^3,\qquad U_s = \left(\frac{2\dot{W}}{\rho A_s}\right)^{1/3}\,} \tag{4} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.x:
Substituting (3) into (2) and using (1), $U_eA_e = U_sA_s$ and $U_e = U_sA_s/A_e$:

$$ T = \rho U_eA_e(U_s - U_e) + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho U_e^2A_e = \rho U_eA_e\left(U_s - \frac{U_e}{2}\right) = \rho A_sU_s\left(U_s - \frac{U_s}{2}\frac{A_s}{A_e}\right) = \rho A_sU_s^2\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\frac{A_s}{A_e}\right). $$

With (4), $\rho A_sU_s^2 = \rho A_s\left(\frac{2\dot{W}}{\rho A_s}\right)^{2/3} = 2^{2/3}\rho^{1/3}\dot{W}^{2/3}A_s^{1/3}$, so

$$ \boxed{\,\frac{T}{\rho^{1/3}\dot{W}^{2/3}A_s^{1/3}} = f\!\left(\frac{A_e}{A_s}\right) = 2^{2/3}\left(1 - \frac{1}{2\,A_e/A_s}\right)\,} \tag{5} $$

chunks.t: Problem - CL9 Submarine Propulsion Device
chunks.h: Phase 4: Interpretation, Limits and Dimensional Check
chunks.x:
- $f$ grows with $A_e/A_s$: a large intake (slow inflow, small suction depression at the inlet) gives the most thrust for a given power, tending to $f \to 2^{2/3} \approx 1.587$ as $A_e/A_s \to \infty$. For $A_e = A_s$, $f = 2^{2/3}/2 \approx 0.794$.
- Thrust grows only as $\dot{W}^{2/3}$: doubling the power gives $2^{2/3} \approx 1.59$ times the thrust, because the extra power goes into a faster jet whose kinetic energy is wasted.
- Dimensions (SI): $[\rho^{1/3}\dot{W}^{2/3}A_s^{1/3}] = (\text{kg/m}^3)^{1/3}(\text{kg m}^2/\text{s}^3)^{2/3}(\text{m}^2)^{1/3} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2 = \text{N}$, so $f$ is dimensionless.
- Numerical check (hypothetical data): $\rho = 1000$ kg/m$^3$, $A_s = 0.05$ m$^2$, $A_e = 0.1$ m$^2$, $\dot{W} = 50$ kW give $U_s = 12.599$ m/s, $U_e = 6.2996$ m/s, $T = 5952.8$ N, and $T/(\rho^{1/3}\dot{W}^{2/3}A_s^{1/3}) = 1.1906 = f(2)$; the energy balance (4) gives back $\dot{W} = 50$ kW.
- Agreement with the official solution: CL9.pdf obtains (1) to (5), $f = 2^{2/3}\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}A_s/A_e\right)$.

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.h: Problem DA1: Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
Official dimensional-analysis sheet of the course, statement transcribed from the sheet, solution after its handwritten key. Part of Topic 6 - Dimensional Analysis.
Method: Π theorem (Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.25), the limit of negligible viscosity (Eq. 6.55) and physical similarity (Eqs. 6.57-6.59).

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
We want to estimate the driving power $W$ necessary to move at a peak velocity $V = 10$ m/s a marine freighter of length $l = 100$ m and total mass at full load $m = 1000$ Tm. For that purpose, a small model of length $l_e = 1$ m, geometrically similar to the real ship, is to be tested on a hydraulic channel. To guide the design of the experiment, follow these steps:

1. Use the dimensional analysis to reduce the parametric dependence of the required power $W$.

2. Write the three equations that need to be satisfied to guarantee physical similarity between the experiment and the full-scale prototype. Verify that it is not possible to find the values of the mass $m_e$ and velocity $V_e$ of the experiment that satisfy simultaneously all three equations, so that complete physical similarity cannot be attained.

3. Assuming that the effect of viscosity on the fluid motion is negligible, determine the values of $m_e$ and $V_e$. Check that the corresponding values of the Reynolds number for both the real prototype and the experiment are indeed sufficiently large for the assumption of negligible viscosity to be a reasonable approximation.

4. If the experimental measurement of the power obtained with the experimental model is $W_e = 10$ W, obtain the value of the driving power $W$ needed to operate the real prototype at the required conditions.

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x: Source: DA1.pdf (page 1, statement and handwritten key). Notes.pdf, Chapter 6: Π theorem, Eq. 6.25; physical similarity, Eqs. 6.57-6.59.

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
- The ship moves at constant velocity on the free surface of water, which is the same liquid in the channel and in the sea: $\rho_e = \rho$, $\mu_e = \mu$, so $\nu_e = \nu = \mu/\rho \simeq 10^{-6}$ m$^2$/s.
- The power goes into the waves made at the free surface (gravity $g$ matters, since the free surface is not flat; Notes.pdf, p. 66) and into the viscous drag ($\mu$ matters, a priori).
- The mass $m$ fixes how deep the hull floats: by Archimedes, the submerged volume is $m/\rho$.
- "Tm" is the metric ton: $m = 1000\ \text{t} = 10^6$ kg.

| Parameter | Meaning | Dimensions | Value (prototype) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $W$ | driving power (unknown) | $ML^2T^{-3}$ | ? |
| $V$ | ship velocity | $LT^{-1}$ | 10 m/s |
| $g$ | gravity | $LT^{-2}$ | 9.81 m/s$^2$ |
| $m$ | mass at full load | $M$ | $10^6$ kg |
| $l$ | ship length | $L$ | 100 m |
| $\rho$ | water density | $ML^{-3}$ | 1000 kg/m$^3$ |
| $\mu$ | water viscosity | $ML^{-1}T^{-1}$ | $10^{-3}$ kg/(m s) |

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
$$ W = W(V, g, m, l, \rho, \mu) $$

There are $n = 6$ governing parameters. Exponent matrix, rows $V$, $l$, $\rho$; columns $L$, $M$, $T$:

$$ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det = 1\,(0\cdot 0 - 0\cdot 1) - 0 + (-1)\,(1\cdot 1 - 0\cdot(-3)) = -1 \neq 0 $$

so $(V, l, \rho)$ have independent dimensions and $k = 3$: there are $n - k = 3$ dimensionless parameters. $(V, l, \rho)$ is chosen because velocity, size and the inertia of the water clearly matter (Notes.pdf, p. 68).

**Power.** $[W] = [\rho]^a[V]^b[l]^c$:

$$ M:\; 1 = a, \qquad T:\; -3 = -b, \qquad L:\; 2 = -3a + b + c $$

so $a = 1$, $b = 3$ and $c = 2 + 3 - 3 = 2$: $\Pi_0 = W/(\rho V^3 l^2)$.

**Gravity.** $[g] = [V]^b[l]^c$ (no mass, so no $\rho$): $T:\; -2 = -b$, $L:\; 1 = b + c$, so $b = 2$, $c = -1$ and $g/(V^2/l)$ is dimensionless; its inverse is the square of the Froude number, $V^2/(gl)$.

**Mass.** $[m] = [\rho]^a[V]^b[l]^c$: $M:\; 1 = a$, $T:\; 0 = -b$, $L:\; 0 = -3a + b + c$, so $a = 1$, $b = 0$, $c = 3$: $m/(\rho l^3)$.

**Viscosity.** $[\mu] = [\rho]^a[V]^b[l]^c$: $M:\; 1 = a$, $T:\; -1 = -b$, $L:\; -1 = -3a + b + c$, so $a = 1$, $b = 1$, $c = 1$: $\mu/(\rho V l)$, the inverse of the Reynolds number.

$$ \frac{W}{\rho V^3 l^2} = f\left(\frac{V^2}{g l}, \frac{m}{\rho l^3}, \frac{\rho V l}{\mu}\right) $$

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
- $V^2/(gl)$ (Froude number squared): inertia against gravity, that is the waves at the free surface.
- $m/(\rho l^3)$: by Archimedes $m/\rho$ is the submerged volume, so this group is proportional to the ratio of the submerged volume to the total volume of the ship.
- $\rho V l/\mu$: the Reynolds number.

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
Model (subscript $e$) and prototype are physically similar when the three governing groups are equal. With the same liquid and the same $g$:

$$ \frac{V^2}{g l} = \frac{V_e^2}{g l_e} \;\Longrightarrow\; V_e = \left(\frac{l_e}{l}\right)^{1/2} V $$

$$ \frac{V l}{\nu} = \frac{V_e l_e}{\nu} \;\Longrightarrow\; V_e = \frac{l}{l_e}\,V $$

$$ \frac{m}{\rho l^3} = \frac{m_e}{\rho l_e^3} \;\Longrightarrow\; m_e = \left(\frac{l_e}{l}\right)^3 m $$

The third equation fixes $m_e$. The first two ask for two different velocities: with $l_e/l = 10^{-2}$, Froude asks for $V_e = 10^{-1}V$ and Reynolds for $V_e = 10^{2}V$. Both hold only if $(l_e/l)^{1/2} = l/l_e$, that is $(l_e/l)^{3/2} = 1$, $l_e = l$: **with the same liquid, no scaled model can be fully similar** (Notes.pdf, p. 71: partial similarity).

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
If viscosity has a negligible effect ($\mathrm{Re}\gg 1$), the group $\rho V l/\mu$ drops out of the law (Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.55):

$$ \frac{W}{\rho V^3 l^2} = f\left(\frac{V^2}{g l}, \frac{m}{\rho l^3}\right) $$

and only the Froude and mass conditions remain:

$$ V_e = \left(\frac{l_e}{l}\right)^{1/2} V = \left(\frac{1}{100}\right)^{1/2}\times 10 = 1\ \text{m/s}, \qquad m_e = \left(\frac{l_e}{l}\right)^3 m = 10^{-6}\times 10^{6} = 1\ \text{kg} $$

Check of the assumption, with $\nu = 10^{-6}$ m$^2$/s:

$$ \mathrm{Re} = \frac{V l}{\nu} = \frac{10\times 100}{10^{-6}} = 10^{9} \gg 1, \qquad \mathrm{Re}_e = \frac{V_e l_e}{\nu} = \frac{1\times 1}{10^{-6}} = 10^{6} \gg 1 $$

Both are very large, so neglecting viscosity is reasonable in the model and in the ship, even though the two Reynolds numbers differ by a factor $10^3$.

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
With the two remaining groups equal, $\Pi_0$ is equal too (Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.58):

$$ \frac{W}{\rho V^3 l^2} = \frac{W_e}{\rho V_e^3 l_e^2} \;\Longrightarrow\; W = \left(\frac{V}{V_e}\right)^3\left(\frac{l}{l_e}\right)^2 W_e $$

$$ W = (10)^3\,(100)^2 \times 10\ \text{W} = 10^{3}\times 10^{4}\times 10 = 10^{8}\ \text{W} = 100\ \text{MW} $$

chunks.t: Problem - DA1 Power of a Marine Freighter
chunks.x:
- Reduced law: $W/(\rho V^3 l^2) = f\left(V^2/(gl),\, m/(\rho l^3),\, \rho V l/\mu\right)$.
- Full similarity needs $V_e = (l_e/l)^{1/2}V$ and $V_e = (l/l_e)V$ at once: impossible for $l_e \neq l$.
- With negligible viscosity: $V_e = 1$ m/s, $m_e = 1$ kg; $\mathrm{Re} = 10^9$, $\mathrm{Re}_e = 10^6$.
- Prototype power: $W = 100$ MW.
- Dimensions: $\rho V^3 l^2$ has $ML^{-3}\cdot L^3T^{-3}\cdot L^2 = ML^2T^{-3}$, a power.
- Scaling check: under Froude similarity $V \propto l^{1/2}$, so $W \propto V^3 l^2 \propto l^{7/2}$, and $100^{7/2} = 10^7$ times 10 W is $10^8$ W, the same.
- Check against the official key: DA1.pdf gives $V_e = 1$ m/s, $m_e = 1$ kg, $\mathrm{Re}\simeq 10^9$, $\mathrm{Re}_e = 10^6$ and $W = 100$ MW, the same results.

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
Official dimensional-analysis sheet of the course (exam of Dec 18, 2012), statement transcribed from the sheet, solution after its handwritten key. Part of Topic 6 - Dimensional Analysis.
Method: Π theorem with $\mu$ in the independent set (Notes.pdf, p. 68), the limit of negligible inertia (Eq. 6.55) and similarity between two liquids in the same pump (Eqs. 6.57-6.59).

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
**PROBLEM 3 (50 minutes)** The system sketched in the figure is designed to steadily pump fluid of constant density $\rho$ and constant viscosity $\mu$ from a reservoir, where the modified pressure has a constant value $P_0$, to another one at pressure $P_0 + \Delta P$ ($\Delta P > 0$). To that end, a pair of parallel belts of length $L$, separated by a distance $h \ll L$, are driven at constant velocities $V_l$ and $V_u$, dragging the liquid towards the large pressure reservoir.

In the forthcoming analysis, the liquid flow can be assumed steady and two-dimensional (spanwise length much larger than $h$). The most important parameters of the system are the liquid volume flux **per unit spanwise length**, $q$, the power needed to drive the system **per unit spanwise length**, $\dot{W}$, and the pump efficiency, $\eta = q\Delta P/\dot{W}$.

*Statement figure (redrawn from DA10.pdf): two parallel belts of length L, a distance h ≪ L apart, driven at V_u and V_l, drag liquid of density ρ and viscosity μ from a reservoir at reduced pressure P_0 to one at P_0 + ΔP*

1. (*3 points*). Use dimensional analysis to simplify the dependence of $q$, $\dot{W}$ and $\eta$, as functions of an appropriately chosen set of parameters governing the operation of the pump.

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
2. (*2 points*). Simplify the resulting dimensionless functions when the inertia of the fluid can be neglected compared to the viscous forces. Note that, in this limit, the fluid density plays a negligible role. In the remainder of the problem, assume that these conditions are satisfied.

A pump with $h = 1$ cm and $L = 20$ cm is calibrated using glycerol, of density $\rho_g = 1260$ kg/m$^3$ and viscosity $\mu_g = 1.41$ kg/(m s), using an overpressure $\Delta P_g = 1$ kPa. During the calibration process, the lower belt is kept at rest, $V_{l,g} = 0$, while the upper belt is driven at several velocities $V_{u,g}$, as indicated in the table below, where the corresponding values of $q_g$, $\dot{W}_g$ and $\eta_g$ are also shown.

| $V_{u,g}$ (cm/s) | $q_g$ (cm$^2$/s) | $\dot{W}_g$ (Watt/m) | $\eta_g$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 10 | 2 | 0.8 | 0.26 |
| 15 | 4.5 | 1.4 | 0.33 |
| 20 | 7 | 2.1 | 0.33 |
| 25 | 9.5 | 3 | 0.32 |
| 30 | 12 | 4 | 0.3 |
| 35 | 14.5 | 5.2 | 0.28 |

The **same pump** is used to deliver a silicone oil, of density $\rho_{oil} = 1100$ kg m$^{-3}$ and viscosity $\mu_{oil} = 5$ kg/(m s), with an overpressure $\Delta P_{oil} = 2$ kPa.

3. (*2 points*). Determine the velocities $V_{l,oil}$ and $V_{u,oil}$ for which the results obtained in the calibration tests can be used to predict the pumping behavior with the silicone oil.

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
4. (*2 points*). Calculate the corresponding values of $q_{oil}$, $\dot{W}_{oil}$ and $\eta_{oil}$.

5. (*1 point*). Discuss the hypothesis of negligible fluid inertia.

Source: DA10.pdf (page 1: statement; page 2: handwritten key). Notes.pdf, Chapter 6: Π theorem, Eq. 6.25; selection of parameters, p. 68; limits, Eq. 6.55; physical similarity, Eqs. 6.57-6.59.

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
- Steady, two-dimensional flow of a liquid with constant $\rho$ and $\mu$; gravity is absorbed in the modified pressure, so only the difference $\Delta P$ enters (Notes.pdf, p. 66).
- All quantities are per unit spanwise length: $[q] = L^2T^{-1}$, $[\dot{W}] = ML^2T^{-3}/L = MLT^{-3}$.
- Recomputing $\eta = q\Delta P/\dot{W}$ from the table: row 1 gives $2\times 10^{-4}\times 10^{3}/0.8 = 0.25$ (printed 0.26) and row 2 gives $4.5\times 10^{-4}\times 10^{3}/1.4 = 0.32$ (printed 0.33); rows 3 to 6 agree with the printed values (0.333, 0.317, 0.300, 0.279).

| Parameter | Dimensions |
| :--- | :--- |
| $q$ | $L^2T^{-1}$ |
| $\dot{W}$ | $MLT^{-3}$ |
| $\eta$ | 1 |
| $\rho$ | $ML^{-3}$ |
| $\mu$ | $ML^{-1}T^{-1}$ |
| $\Delta P$ | $ML^{-1}T^{-2}$ |
| $V_u$, $V_l$ | $LT^{-1}$ |
| $L$, $h$ | $L$ |

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
$$ q = f_1(\rho, \mu, \Delta P, V_u, V_l, L, h), \qquad \dot{W} = f_2(\dots), \qquad \eta = f_3(\dots) $$

$n = 7$. The key takes $(\mu, V_u, h)$, natural for a viscous pump. Rows $\mu(-1, 1, -1)$, $V_u(1, 0, -1)$, $h(1, 0, 0)$ in $(L, M, T)$; only $\mu$ has mass, so expanding along the $M$ column, $\det = -1\cdot\left(1\cdot 0 - (-1)\cdot 1\right) = -1 \neq 0$: $k = 3$, and $n - k = 4$ groups remain.

**Flux.** $[q] = [\mu]^a[V_u]^b[h]^c$: $M:\; 0 = a$; $T:\; -1 = -b$; $L:\; 2 = b + c$; so the scale is $V_u h$.

**Power.** $[\dot{W}] = [\mu]^a[V_u]^b[h]^c$: $M:\; 1 = a$; $T:\; -3 = -a - b$, $b = 2$; $L:\; 1 = -a + b + c$, $c = 0$; so the scale is $\mu V_u^2$.

**Density.** $[\rho] = [\mu]^a[V_u]^b[h]^c$: $M:\; 1 = a$; $T:\; 0 = -1 - b$, $b = -1$; $L:\; -3 = -1 - 1 + c$, $c = -1$: the group $\rho V_u h/\mu$, a Reynolds number.

**Pressure.** $[\Delta P] = [\mu]^a[V_u]^b[h]^c$: $M:\; 1 = a$; $T:\; -2 = -1 - b$, $b = 1$; $L:\; -1 = -1 + 1 + c$, $c = -1$: the group $h\Delta P/(\mu V_u)$.

**Belts and geometry.** $V_l/V_u$ and $L/h$.

$$ \frac{q}{V_u h} = \Pi_q\left(\frac{\rho V_u h}{\mu}, \frac{h\Delta P}{\mu V_u}, \frac{V_l}{V_u}, \frac{L}{h}\right), \quad \frac{\dot{W}}{\mu V_u^2} = \Pi_W(\dots), \quad \eta = \eta(\dots) $$

with the same four arguments.

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
When inertia is negligible against viscous forces, the density drops out ($\rho V_u h/\mu \to 0$; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.55):

$$ \frac{q}{V_u h} = \Pi_q\left(\frac{h\Delta P}{\mu V_u}, \frac{V_l}{V_u}, \frac{L}{h}\right), \quad \frac{\dot{W}}{\mu V_u^2} = \Pi_W\left(\frac{h\Delta P}{\mu V_u}, \frac{V_l}{V_u}, \frac{L}{h}\right), \quad \eta = \eta\left(\frac{h\Delta P}{\mu V_u}, \frac{V_l}{V_u}, \frac{L}{h}\right) $$

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.h: Physical Similarity: from Glycerol to Silicone Oil
chunks.x:
The pump is the same, so $L/h$ is the same. The other two groups must be equal.

**Lower belt.**

$$ \frac{V_{l,oil}}{V_{u,oil}} = \frac{V_{l,g}}{V_{u,g}} = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; V_{l,oil} = 0 $$

**Upper belt.** The same $h$ cancels:

$$ \frac{h\Delta P_{oil}}{\mu_{oil}V_{u,oil}} = \frac{h\Delta P_g}{\mu_g V_{u,g}} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{V_{u,oil}}{V_{u,g}} = \frac{\mu_g}{\mu_{oil}}\,\frac{\Delta P_{oil}}{\Delta P_g} = \frac{1.41}{5}\times\frac{2}{1} = 0.564 $$

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
With all groups equal, the dimensionless outputs are equal:

$$ \frac{q_{oil}}{V_{u,oil}h} = \frac{q_g}{V_{u,g}h} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{q_{oil}}{q_g} = \frac{V_{u,oil}}{V_{u,g}} = 0.564 $$

$$ \frac{\dot{W}_{oil}}{\mu_{oil}V_{u,oil}^2} = \frac{\dot{W}_g}{\mu_g V_{u,g}^2} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{\dot{W}_{oil}}{\dot{W}_g} = \frac{\mu_{oil}}{\mu_g}\left(\frac{V_{u,oil}}{V_{u,g}}\right)^2 = \frac{5}{1.41}\times 0.564^2 = 3.546\times 0.3181 = 1.128 $$

$$ \eta_{oil} = \eta_g $$

Check: $\eta_{oil}/\eta_g = (q_{oil}/q_g)(\Delta P_{oil}/\Delta P_g)/(\dot{W}_{oil}/\dot{W}_g) = 0.564\times 2/1.128 = 1$. The $\eta_{oil}$ column copies the printed $\eta_g$, as the key does; from $q\Delta P/\dot{W}$ the first two rows would read 0.25 and 0.32.

| $V_{u,g}$ (cm/s) | $V_{u,oil}$ (cm/s) | $q_{oil}$ (cm$^2$/s) | $\dot{W}_{oil}$ (W/m) | $\eta_{oil}$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 10 | 5.64 | 1.128 | 0.902 | 0.26 |
| 15 | 8.46 | 2.538 | 1.579 | 0.33 |
| 20 | 11.28 | 3.948 | 2.369 | 0.33 |
| 25 | 14.10 | 5.358 | 3.384 | 0.32 |
| 30 | 16.92 | 6.768 | 4.512 | 0.30 |
| 35 | 19.74 | 8.178 | 5.866 | 0.28 |

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
The plain Reynolds number of the calibration is not small: $\rho_g V_{u,g}h/\mu_g = 1260\times 0.10\times 0.01/1.41 = 0.89$ at the lowest speed and $3.1$ at the highest. The key compares inertia and viscosity in the **slender** channel ($h \ll L$), where the convective term is smaller than the viscous one by the extra factor $h/L$, so the relevant number is the reduced Reynolds number $(\rho V_u h/\mu)(h/L)$. This criterion belongs to the slender viscous flows of Chapter 7 of the notes (an **extension** here). With $h/L = 1/20$:

$$ \text{glycerol: } 0.89\times\frac{1}{20} = 0.045 \;\le\; \frac{\rho_g V_{u,g}h}{\mu_g}\,\frac{h}{L} \;\le\; 3.13\times\frac{1}{20} = 0.156 $$

$$ \text{oil: } \frac{1100\times 0.0564\times 0.01}{5}\times\frac{1}{20} = 0.0062 \;\le\; \frac{\rho_{oil}V_{u,oil}h}{\mu_{oil}}\,\frac{h}{L} \;\le\; \frac{1100\times 0.1974\times 0.01}{5}\times\frac{1}{20} = 0.022 $$

Both are small, more so for the oil, so neglecting inertia is a good approximation, and the calibration can be transferred to the oil.

chunks.t: Problem - DA10 Two-Belt Viscous Pump
chunks.x:
- Reduced laws: $q/(V_uh)$, $\dot{W}/(\mu V_u^2)$ and $\eta$ are functions of $\rho V_uh/\mu$, $h\Delta P/(\mu V_u)$, $V_l/V_u$, $L/h$; without inertia, of the last three only.
- Similar operation with oil: $V_{l,oil} = 0$, $V_{u,oil} = 0.564\,V_{u,g}$.
- Oil performance: $q_{oil} = 0.564\,q_g$, $\dot{W}_{oil} = 1.128\,\dot{W}_g$, $\eta_{oil} = \eta_g$ (table above).
- Inertia: reduced Reynolds number 0.045-0.156 (glycerol) and 0.006-0.022 (oil).
- Dimensions: $\mu V_u^2$ is $ML^{-1}T^{-1}\cdot L^2T^{-2} = MLT^{-3}$, a power per unit length; $h\Delta P/(\mu V_u)$ is $L\cdot ML^{-1}T^{-2}/(ML^{-1}T^{-1}\cdot LT^{-1}) = 1$.
- Check against the official key: DA10.pdf gives $V_{l,oil} = 0$, $V_{u,oil}/V_{u,g} = 0.564$, $q_{oil}/q_g = 0.564$, $\dot{W}_{oil}/\dot{W}_g = 1.128$ and the same table, with the inertia ranges 0.045-0.156 and 0.0062-0.022.

chunks.t: Problem - DA11 Power of a Wave Generator
chunks.h: Problem DA11: Power of a Wave Generator
chunks.x:
Official dimensional-analysis sheet of the course (exam of Jan 14, 2013), statement transcribed from the sheet, solution after its handwritten key. Part of Topic 6 - Dimensional Analysis.
Method: Π theorem (Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.25), the limit of negligible viscosity (Eq. 6.55) and Froude similarity (Eqs. 6.57-6.59).

chunks.t: Problem - DA11 Power of a Wave Generator
chunks.x:
**PROBLEM 3 (45 minutes)** The figure below illustrates a simple mechanism to generate periodic gravity waves in a pool of liquid (density $\rho$ and viscosity $\mu$), with undisturbed height $H$. The waves are driven by the harmonic motion of the lateral confining wall perpendicular to itself, with amplitude $A$ and frequency $\omega$.

*Statement figure (redrawn from DA11.pdf): above, the pool of liquid (ρ, μ) of undisturbed depth H; below, the lateral wall moved harmonically, x = A cos(2πωt), by the power Ẇ, generating gravity waves*

1. (*4 points*). Use dimensional analysis to simplify the dependence of the power needed to drive the generator, $\dot{W}$, as a function of the governing parameters $(\rho, \mu, A, \omega, H, g)$.

2. (*1 point*). Simplify the resulting dimensionless function for the case of negligible viscous forces. In the remainder of the problem, assume that this condition is satisfied.

To characterize the requirements of a new wave generator to be installed in a large water channel (subindex p), a scale model (subindex m) with $H_m/H_p = 1/20$ is tested in the lab using water as working fluid. Knowing that the wave frequency required in the water channel is $\omega_p = 1/6$ s$^{-1}$,
